pr_title: Support TLS Resume with client certificates on Linux
pr_body:
Closes #94561.

This PR enables TLS resume on Linux if client certificate is provided. The feature is triggered if local certificate selection routine manages to select a certificate, i.e. either of these situations:
- ClientCertificateContext
- LocalCertificateSelectionCallback returns non-null certificate on first call (otherwise selection based on server cert/acceptable issuers is assumed and fresh SSL_CTX is always used)
- ClientCertificates collection has at least one certificate (and first one with private key is used)

The feature is enabled by caching SSL_CTX as before, certificate thumbprint has been added to the cache key to mirror what we do on Windows. The caching code has been reused from MsQuicConfiguration cache (and in further PR can be unified with the caching code we have for SslStream credentials on Windows).

I stressed the caching code under a dedicated program, there does not seem to be any leakage.
pr_comments:
Looks like TLS 1.3 works as well. (Windows server, Linux client, client cert required)

![image](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/assets/32671551/898a1ad6-6b41-4100-ab3e-2ebc85abc1c1)

> I need to do a bit more testing (can't test TLS 1.3 resumption against .NET Linux server yet, as we support only stateful resumption yet).

I don't quite understand the comment. I thought we only support stateless e.g. tickets to avoid large server cache. But I would also think that it does not matter e.g. the resumption is possible in either way.

> > I need to do a bit more testing (can't test TLS 1.3 resumption against .NET Linux server yet, as we support only stateful resumption yet).
> 
> I don't quite understand the comment. I thought we only support stateless e.g. tickets to avoid large server cache. But I would also think that it does not matter e.g. the resumption is possible in either way.

I meant that Linux .NET server does not issue resumption tokens in TLS 1.3, so I had to test against different server (Windows in this case).

Edit: my bad, it turns out that the resumption ticket was not transmitted because we close the connection without actually transmitting any user data, adding a ping-pong to the tests fixed the problem.

issue_context.title: Support TLS Resume with client certificates on Linux
issue_context.body:
From https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/94080#issuecomment-1791564430

> [...] mTLS is one of the most common mechanisms for S2S (service to service) calls. In AAD alone, there are >300 billion mTLS calls every day. (and this is just internal traffic). Our public facing flows also have significant mTLS : https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/authentication/concept-certificate-based-authentication. Perf improvements in mTLS code paths can save millions of dollars in TLS costs.

Mutual authentication should be already fully supported on Windows, but we currently don't support it on Linux (and not at all on MacOS).
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/58e03495cf2385f7104acb017df621984d4b7036/src/libraries/Common/src/Interop/Unix/System.Security.Cryptography.Native/Interop.OpenSsl.cs#L305-L319

This will need some more thinking and testing. Specifically against cases when we unintentionally restore session with wrong certificate. When we only have one identity for any given server it is pretty simple. But if we have multiple services running on different port (SslStream does not have access to EndPoint) or if we want to maintain multiple identities to same service things do get more tricky.

However, cases where only 1 client certificate is provided (whether via ClientCertificates collection, or CertificateContext, or perhaps even the certificate selection callback) may be simple and safe to implement.

review_comments: I think we should aslo add tests to verify that similar but not same sessions are _not_ resumed. So far we were rending on schannel so I think the test coverage is really weak. Since we implemented our own logic I think we need more tests.
Why not just define the P/Invoke in terms of the SafeHandle then?

We don't have SafeHandle type (yet) for SSL_SESSION and here would be the only usage that would need it. Unless you think we should go the extra mile to be sure, I would like to keep it this way to avoid the extra allocations and P/Invokes for the SafeHandle.

I think I just got confused by the comment.  It's doing the AddRef/Release pattern that a P/Invoke in terms of a SafeHandle already does, and the comment sounded like "we need to do this addref/release because we're going to pass `ssl.DangerousGetHandle()`"; but instead it's that you want the SSL* to stay up-refd while you get, use, and discard the SSL_SESSION*.  Which the comment does say, upon a re-read.

should we consider everything that get set on context -- like CipherSuite or EncryptonPolicy? Let say there are two clients with same client certificate and disjoint cipher suites. We could resume now session that does not match the requested parameters, right?

We don't need to consider all of them. We disable TLS resume if we diverge from the default settings.

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/13e6f9265d95e8a2df1db19972125ea5d740a1d2/src/libraries/Common/src/Interop/Unix/System.Security.Cryptography.Native/Interop.OpenSsl.cs#L296

in order to support these, we would have to unify the caching mechanism between client and server SSL_CTX instances to avoid duplicate efforts.
What are the implications of a collision here, either by “luck” or a malicious client?
Ah wait, I am assuming the client certificate has a valid chain at this point.

The certificate is taken from SslStreamCertificateContext, so the (valid) chain should be already built by then.

In case of collision, we would attempt to reuse a session established with a different certificate. Note that the sessions are later cached per-host, so we would reuse sessions to the same host only.

Also note that this is the same mechanism we use in e.g. 

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/1815306c1b325a66189511f3ddecd45638c47681/src/libraries/System.Net.Security/src/System/Net/Security/SslSessionsCache.cs#L99-L107
While the same certificate hash code is very unlikely (and we use it already) I'm wondering if that is good enough. Any thoughts on that @bartonjs ?
Note that we moved to using SHA256 here https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/102656#discussion_r1613804904, I think we should (in separate PR) do this for other places as well.
Discussed offline, SHA256 is good enough.
